lessons.title: Credit, Confidence, and Contagion: How a Local Problem Goes Global

body.text: A crisis spreads not because everyone is exposed to the problem, but because nobody can tell who is.

children.text: On 21 September 2018, DSP Mutual Fund sold a block of commercial paper issued by DHFL, a large housing finance company, at a noticeably higher yield than the market expected. DHFL had not missed a single payment. It did not matter. Coming weeks after IL&FS began defaulting, the sale looked like someone who knew something was heading for the exit. DHFL's share price fell about 42% that day and the Nifty dropped more than 100 points.
One fund selling one bond, and a whole sector was shaken. That is the subject of this lesson: the three forces that turn a local problem into a system-wide one.

children.text: Force 1: Credit, the Fuel
Crises almost never start with people losing their own money. They start with people losing borrowed money. Borrowing lets you control more assets than your own capital could buy, and that is called
leverage
. It is measured as total assets divided by your own equity.

markDefs.definition: Using borrowed money to hold more assets than your own capital alone would allow. Leverage multiplies both gains and losses on your own money.

children.text: Leverage is harmless in good times and brutal in bad ones, because it multiplies every loss on your assets into a much bigger loss on your own money.

body.caption: Leverage = Total assets ÷ Own equity. The wipeout point is a fall of 1 ÷ Leverage.
Same ₹1 crore of assets, three levels of borrowing
headers: Asset fall that wipes out own money

body.title: How much of your own money survives a small fall in assets

children.text: Look at the 30x line. A 3% dip, the kind of move the Nifty makes in a bad week, leaves just 10% of the owner's money. A 4% dip leaves nothing. Lehman Brothers reported leverage of 30.7x in November 2007, with a large share of those assets tied to US real estate. It did not need a catastrophe to fail, only a modest fall in property values.

body.title: Find the Wipeout Point
body.prompt: A non-bank lender holds ₹5,000 crore of loans funded by ₹200 crore of its own equity and the rest in borrowings. By what percentage must the value of its loans fall to wipe out its equity completely?
body.explanation: Leverage = ₹5,000 crore ÷ ₹200 crore = 25x. The wipeout point is 1 ÷ 25 = 4%. If just 4% of its loans turn bad, a ₹200 crore loss, the lender's equity is gone.

body.text: The same math applies to you. If you buy shares using a margin trading facility (MTF) from your broker, or trade futures on the NSE, you are using leverage. A position at 4x leverage loses 20% of your own capital on a 5% move in the stock. Crises punish leveraged investors first and hardest.

children.text: Force 2: Confidence, the Spark
Most financial firms fund long-term assets with short-term borrowing. An NBFC might give 15-year home loans while funding itself with
commercial paper
that must be repaid every few months. As each paper matures, it simply borrows again. This is called a
rollover

markDefs.definition: Short-term unsecured borrowing, usually for up to one year, issued by companies and NBFCs and bought mostly by mutual funds, banks and corporate treasuries.
Repaying maturing short-term debt by raising fresh short-term debt. A lender that relies on rollovers is safe only while investors remain willing to lend again.

children.text: Rollover depends on one thing: lenders believing they will be repaid. The moment that belief cracks, lenders stop rolling over, and even a profitable firm can run out of cash within weeks. Confidence is not a soft, emotional extra in finance. It is the funding.

body.title: Short-term funding markets: normal times vs crisis times

columns.label: Normal times
points: Lenders assume most borrowers are sound
Maturing debt is rolled over automatically
Borrowers are priced on their own credit quality
Cash is lent out freely because idle cash earns nothing

columns.label: Crisis times
points: Lenders cannot tell sound borrowers from weak ones
Rollovers are refused or priced at punishing rates
Every borrower in the sector is treated as suspect
Everyone hoards cash, so markets freeze

children.text: This is exactly why DHFL's shares collapsed without a default. IL&FS had shown that a well-rated infrastructure lender could fail. Investors then asked a simple question about every NBFC funded by short-term paper: are you next? When DSP sold DHFL paper cheaply, the market took it as an answer.

body.label: What Confidence Can Do Even to a Sound Bank
body.context: After Lehman failed, rumours about ICICI Bank's exposure sent customers to ATMs in several cities. The RBI publicly stated the bank had adequate liquidity and arranged cash for it, and the Finance Ministry backed that assurance. The run faded because a credible authority restored confidence.

children.text: Force 3: Contagion, the Spread
Once credit has built up and confidence breaks,
contagion
carries the damage outward. It travels through five main channels.

markDefs.definition: The spread of financial distress from one institution, market or country to others, including ones that had no direct link to the original problem.

cells: A firm that lent to the failing firm takes a loss
Reserve Primary Fund held $785 million of Lehman paper and its NAV fell to $0.97 in September 2008
Forced sellers dump assets, pushing prices down for every other holder
DSP's sale of DHFL paper in September 2018 reset prices for NBFC debt across the market
Lenders refuse to roll over debt for a whole category of borrowers
NBFCs struggled to roll over commercial paper after IL&FS defaulted in 2018
Investors reassess any firm or country that looks similar
The "Fragile Five" label in August 2013 grouped India with Brazil, Indonesia, South Africa and Turkey
Global investors pull money from riskier markets all at once
FIIs sold a net ₹52,987 crore of Indian equities in 2008

body.title: From a New York bankruptcy to an Indian ATM queue

events.title: Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy
events.description: The fourth largest US investment bank collapses after lenders refuse to keep funding it.

events.title: A "safe" money market fund breaks
events.description: The Reserve Primary Fund, holding $785 million of Lehman paper, cuts its NAV to $0.97. Redemption requests pass $40 billion within two days. Direct exposure has become a run.

events.title: Short-term funding markets freeze
events.description: Investors flee money market funds, so those funds stop buying commercial paper. Companies with no link to Lehman struggle to fund day-to-day operations.

events.title: Rumours hit ICICI Bank
events.description: Worries about ICICI Bank's Lehman exposure trigger ATM queues in India. The RBI and Finance Ministry step in to reassure depositors.

events.title: The RBI floods the system with cash
events.description: The RBI cuts the cash reserve ratio (CRR) from 9% in stages to 5% by January 2009, releasing liquidity so Indian banks keep lending.

events.title: Foreign money leaves India
events.description: FIIs pull a net ₹52,987 crore out of Indian equities, and the Sensex ends the year down about half.

body.title: Spot the Channel
body.question: In 2013, foreign investors sold Indian bonds and equities heavily, even though India had no banking collapse, simply because India shared features with other emerging markets that looked vulnerable. Which contagion channel is this mainly?
body.explanation: This is the wake-up call channel. Investors grouped countries with large current account deficits and dependence on foreign money, the "Fragile Five", and pulled out of all of them together. India was not directly exposed to anyone else's losses. It simply looked similar. Foreign capital flight then followed as the result.

body.title: Name the Mechanism
body.textWithBlank: When an NBFC repays maturing commercial paper by issuing fresh commercial paper, it is relying on a ___.
body.explanation: A rollover. It works only while lenders stay confident. When confidence breaks, rollovers stop, and a firm with long-term assets and short-term funding can run out of cash quickly.

body.title: Your Debt Fund and Someone Else's Default
body.scenario: You hold units in a short duration debt mutual fund. News breaks that a large NBFC, which your fund does not hold, has defaulted on its commercial paper. Over the next week, yields on paper from several other NBFCs jump, and your fund's NAV slips 0.8% even though none of its holdings has defaulted.
body.prompt: Using the three forces from this lesson, explain why your NAV fell, and list what you would check before deciding whether to stay invested.
body.modelAnswer: Why the NAV fell: this is contagion through the wake-up call and fire sale channels. After one NBFC defaulted, investors began doubting similar borrowers, confidence broke, and yields on other NBFC paper rose. Debt fund NAVs are marked to market, so when yields on paper your fund holds go up, the prices of that paper fall, and your NAV falls even without any default. What to check: first, the fund's monthly portfolio disclosure on the AMC website or its factsheet, to see how much sits in NBFC paper and in lower rated instruments. Second, how concentrated the fund is in any single issuer or group. Third, the credit ratings of its top holdings and whether any have been put on watch. Fourth, whether the fund has the option to create a segregated portfolio under SEBI rules if a holding does default. If the fund holds mostly high rated, well-diversified paper and none of its issuers is in real trouble, a mark-to-market dip from contagion often reverses once confidence returns. If it is concentrated in weak NBFC paper, the risk is real, not just sentiment.

body.title: Go deeper: why even strong lenders stop lending in a panic

children.text: Picture a bank treasury with ₹500 crore of spare cash on a Monday in late September 2008. Normally it would lend that overnight to other banks and earn interest. Today it faces three problems.
It cannot see other banks' exposure to Lehman, so any borrower might be the next one to fail.
Its own depositors might panic tomorrow, so cash in hand is suddenly worth more than the interest it would earn.
If it lends and the borrower fails, the treasury head gets blamed. If it hoards and misses some interest, nobody gets blamed.

Every bank reasons the same way at the same time, so the interbank market freezes even though no single bank made an unreasonable choice. This is why central banks, not private lenders, have to break the freeze by offering cash to the whole system, as the RBI did through its CRR cuts.

points: Credit is the fuel: leverage multiplies small asset losses into large equity losses, and the wipeout point is a fall of 1 ÷ leverage
Confidence is the spark: firms that fund long-term assets with short-term borrowing survive only while lenders keep rolling over their debt
Contagion is the spread, through direct exposure, fire sales, funding freezes, wake-up calls and foreign capital flight
A firm does not need to default to be hit by a crisis; DHFL lost about 42% in a day in 2018 on doubts alone
Credible action by central banks and governments, like the RBI backing ICICI Bank and cutting the CRR in 2008, is often what stops contagion
